# Overview of Part 01

Welcome to **Part 01** of the End-to-End R Programming Curriculum! This document brings together the core concepts from:

1. `01_variables_and_datatypes.R` — Variables, Atomic Types, Coercion, Operators, and Special Values (`NA`, `NaN`, `Inf`, `NULL`).
2. `02_data_structures.R` — Vectors, Factors, Matrices, Arrays, Lists, and Data Frames.
3. `03_control_flow_and_functions.R` — Conditionals, Loops, Custom Functions, and the `apply` family.

---

# Variables, Atomic Data Types & Operators

## Variable Assignment & Atomic Types

In R, everything is an object, and every atomic vector is built from one of six fundamental types (`logical`, `integer`, `double`/`numeric`, `complex`, `character`, `raw`).

```{r atomic-types}
# Variable assignment
learning_rate <- 0.015       # double (numeric)
epochs        <- 150L        # integer (note the 'L' suffix)
model_name    <- "XGBoost"   # character
converged     <- TRUE        # logical

# Inspecting class vs low-level storage type
type_summary <- data.frame(
  Object = c("learning_rate", "epochs", "model_name", "converged"),
  Class  = c(class(learning_rate), class(epochs), class(model_name), class(converged)),
  Typeof = c(typeof(learning_rate), typeof(epochs), typeof(model_name), typeof(converged))
)
knitr::kable(type_summary, caption = "Comparison of `class()` and `typeof()` across core R objects")
```

## Type Coercion Hierarchy

When you combine mixed types inside a single atomic vector `c()`, R implicitly coerces all elements to the most flexible type following this hierarchy:

$$\text{logical} \rightarrow \text{integer} \rightarrow \text{double (numeric)} \rightarrow \text{complex} \rightarrow \text{character}$$

```{r coercion}
mixed_1 <- c(TRUE, 10L, 3.14)       # Coerced to numeric (double)
mixed_2 <- c(TRUE, 10L, "R_Rocks")  # Coerced to character

cat("mixed_1:", mixed_1, "| typeof:", typeof(mixed_1), "\n")
cat("mixed_2:", mixed_2, "| typeof:", typeof(mixed_2), "\n")
```

## Handling Special Values (`NA`, `NaN`, `Inf`, `NULL`)

```{r special-values}
measurements <- c(14.2, 18.9, NA, 21.4, 16.0, NA, 19.5)

cat("Total length:       ", length(measurements), "\n")
cat("Missing count:      ", sum(is.na(measurements)), "\n")
cat("Complete cases mean:", round(mean(measurements, na.rm = TRUE), 2), "\n")
```

# Core Data Structures

R's data structures are classified by dimensionality and type homogeneity:

| Dimension | Homogeneous (Single Type) | Heterogeneous (Mixed Types) |
|:---|:---|:---|
| **1D** | Atomic Vector (`c()`) | List (`list()`) |
| **2D** | Matrix (`matrix()`) | Data Frame (`data.frame()`, `tibble()`) |
| **nD** | Array (`array()`) | — |

## Vectors & Indexing

R uses **1-based indexing** and supports four powerful ways to subset any structure:

```{r vector-subsetting}
temps <- c(Mon = 22.5, Tue = 25.1, Wed = 19.8, Thu = 28.4, Fri = 30.2, Sat = 27.0, Sun = 24.3)

# 1. Positive integers
temps[c(1, 5)]

# 2. Negative integers (exclude weekend)
temps[-c(6, 7)]

# 3. Logical mask (days above 25C)
temps[temps > 25]

# 4. Character names
temps[c("Wed", "Sat")]
```

## Factors for Categorical Data

```{r factors}
risk_levels <- factor(
  c("Medium", "Low", "Critical", "High", "Low", "Critical", "Medium"),
  levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High", "Critical"),
  ordered = TRUE
)
table(risk_levels)
```

## Matrices & Linear Algebra

```{r matrices}
# Solving a system of linear equations: A * x = b
# 3x + 2y = 18
#  x + 4y = 16
A <- matrix(c(3, 2, 1, 4), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
b <- c(18, 16)

solution <- solve(A, b)
names(solution) <- c("x", "y")
print(solution)
```

## Lists & Data Frames

```{r dataframes}
portfolio_df <- data.frame(
  ticker   = c("AAPL", "MSFT", "GOOGL", "NVDA", "AMZN"),
  sector   = factor(c("Tech", "Tech", "Comm", "Semiconductors", "Consumer")),
  shares   = c(50L, 40L, 60L, 80L, 45L),
  price    = c(195.2, 420.5, 175.8, 125.4, 185.0),
  dividend = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
)

portfolio_df$market_value <- portfolio_df$shares * portfolio_df$price
 portfolio_df <- portfolio_df[order(-portfolio_df$market_value), ]
knitr::kable(portfolio_df, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Sorted Investment Portfolio Data Frame")
```

# Control Flow, Functions & Vectorization

## Writing Clean, Reusable Functions

```{r custom-functions}
#' Robust Z-Score Standardization (using Median and MAD)
#' @param x Numeric vector
#' @param na.rm Logical; remove NA values before calculation
robust_zscore <- function(x, na.rm = TRUE) {
  stopifnot(is.numeric(x))
  med <- median(x, na.rm = na.rm)
  mad_val <- mad(x, na.rm = na.rm)
  if (mad_val == 0) stop("MAD is zero; cannot standardize constant vector.")
  (x - med) / mad_val
}

raw_signal <- c(10, 12, 11, 13, 12, 95, 11, 10) # 95 is an extreme outlier
round(robust_zscore(raw_signal), 2)
```

## The `apply` Family in Action

```{r apply-family}
# Compute multiple summary statistics across numeric columns of iris
iris_numeric <- iris[, 1:4]

summary_matrix <- vapply(
  iris_numeric,
  FUN = function(col) {
    c(Mean = mean(col), SD = sd(col), Median = median(col), IQR = IQR(col))
  },
  FUN.VALUE = numeric(4)
)

knitr::kable(round(summary_matrix, 2), caption = "Type-safe summary table using `vapply()` on `iris`")
```

---

# Summary & Key Takeaways

- **Always prefer `<-` for assignment** and `TRUE` / `FALSE` over `T` / `F`.
- **Understand vectorization**: operations in R act element-wise across entire vectors without needing explicit `for` loops.
- **When writing loops**, pre-allocate your output vector (`numeric(n)`, `vector("list", n)`) and iterate with `seq_along(x)`.
- **Use `[[` or `$`** to extract elements from a list or data frame, and `[` to slice subsets while keeping the container structure.
